response.text:
Krook’s shop erupts in a grotesque blaze of “spontaneous combustion,” and in the sooty aftermath the Smallweeds pounce upon his papers while the case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce drones on, eating years and fortunes. Into this murk Inspector Bucket quietly begins to move, even as the implacable lawyer Tulkinghorn tightens a net around Lady Dedlock’s old secret—her youthful love for the law-writer Nemo and the birth of Esther, raised in ignorance by a stern aunt. George Rouncewell is driven into debt by the parasitic Smallweed and trapped by Tulkinghorn’s threats; Esther, laid low by smallpox while nursing afflicted children, recovers with scars and is sent to convalesce at Boythorn’s, only to meet Lady Dedlock, who reveals herself to be her mother and then submits to Tulkinghorn’s cold ultimatum of public exposure.

Around them, the domestic threads entwine and darken: Richard Carstone and Ada secretly marry, and under the vampiric guidance of Mr. Vholes the suit becomes Richard’s fixed idea, draining his spirits, money, and prospects. Guppy blunders in and out bearing scraps of gossip and handkerchiefs, while Mr. Skimpole’s perfumed innocence proves as mercenary as any bill of costs. Tulkinghorn is found shot in his rooms just when he seems poised to disclose Lady Dedlock’s story; Bucket, with inexorable courtesy, unravels the case and arrests Hortense, the dismissed French maid, whose jealous malice drove her to the crime.

Lady Dedlock, believing herself accused of murder as well as shame, flees in terror from Chesney Wold, leaving Sir Leicester to suffer a paralytic stroke but still declare her blameless and beloved. Esther joins Bucket in a night-long chase through fog and sleet that ends at a wretched London churchyard, where they find Lady Dedlock dead upon Nemo’s grave. Sir Leicester survives, diminished yet constant, and the house at Chesney Wold settles into a hush, its grandeur peopled by echoes, its life kept going by Volumnia’s stately flutterings, George’s faithful attendance, and Boythorn’s uproarious feud conducted for show more than malice.

A ray of hope briefly pierces Chancery’s gloom when a late will, singed and forgotten among Krook’s rubbish, is produced, suggesting the vast fortune may yet be ordered aright. But when the matter finally “comes on,” it appears that costs have consumed the whole estate; Jarndyce and Jarndyce collapses with a laugh in court and the words, “Estate exhausted.” Richard, undone by the news yet steadfastly gentle, dies in Ada’s arms, naming their newborn son after himself and blessing the friends who never deserted him. The lesson, as bleak as any fog in Lincoln’s Inn, is set against the tender light of the household: Ada bears her sorrow with unselfish courage, and Esther’s compassion turns grief into service.

Allan Woodcourt, the seafaring surgeon who comforted Jo and tended the poor, loves Esther through illness and disfigurement; Jarndyce, the most generous of guardians, releases her from their engagement with a father’s joy and gifts them a small cottage he has secretly adorned to her tastes, naming it “Bleak House.” Guppy’s comic self-importance has one last bow, and Mrs. Jellyby’s telescopic philanthropy survives as the rights of women replace Borrioboola-Gha, while Caddy toils happily at her teaching and tends a deaf and dumb child with inexhaustible patience. George is reconciled to his ironmaster brother and serves Sir Leicester as a loyal equerry; Bucket resumes his watchful rounds; the Smallweeds wither into their own meanness.

Esther’s story closes years later among roses and children at the new Bleak House, where Allan’s rounds bring comfort to the living and where Jarndyce is father and friend, still “my guardian” in her heart. She has learned that the law’s chancery can corrode fortunes and enthrone delay, but that steadfast kindness, daily duty, and homely love can build a truer estate. The great cause is dissolved into ashes, yet the little commonwealth of friends endures, proving that in a world of fog and paper, mercy and humanity remain the only clear air.
